title: The Cabinet Secretary as constitutional guardian — and why Lord Case wants a written constitution
label: 16 September 2026 · Constitution Committee
summary: Lord Case, former Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Civil Service, gave evidence to the Constitution Committee about the role of the Cabinet Secretary in the UK constitution. He described the Cabinet Secretary as a 'tier 2' constitutional guardian, subordinate to the Prime Minister and monarch, and discussed the importance of trust, confidentiality and the 'golden triangle' of advisers. He argued that the current unwritten constitution relies too heavily on the 'good chaps' theory and that the UK should move towards a more codified, written constitution, though he acknowledged that achieving this would be extremely difficult outside a major crisis.

chapters.title: The Cabinet Secretary as a tier 2 guardian
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case sees the Cabinet Secretary as a supporting constitutional guardian, not a principal, whose power depends on trust and access to predecessors.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Lord Case. Our inquiry is into the UK's constitutional safeguards. How would you describe the Cabinet Secretary's role in the constitution? Is the Cabinet Secretary a constitutional guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes, but I'd call it a tier 2 guardian, not tier 1. The real tier 1 guardians are the monarch and the Prime Minister. The Cabinet Secretary, like the PM's principal private secretary and the sovereign's private secretary, doesn't have much independent legal status. We support the principals. My main job is advising the Prime Minister on constitutional matters, and occasionally I'd deal with the sovereign's private secretary.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You served under four Prime Ministers in quick succession, plus a reign change and a pandemic. How did you navigate all that?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Most of those lessons are about party politics, not the constitution. But yes, there was a lot going on. The key is trusting relationships with key colleagues and access to predecessors. I was trained by Lord Hennessy, so I had some academic grounding. One example: when Boris Johnson's government was collapsing, someone suggested calling a general election to save him. I had to pull out the Lascelles principles and the 1950 'Senex' letter to explain why that was a bad idea and why the sovereign might refuse. You need to be able to stand up to a Prime Minister or Cabinet Minister and say, 'Here are the facts and my judgment.'

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So the Cabinet Secretary needs to be strong enough to stand up to an outspoken Cabinet Minister?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes, you do. You need to be confident about what's fact, what's judgment, and what's opinion. Having access to predecessors and good relationships with critical colleagues, like the sovereign's private secretary, is essential. I was lucky: I'd been principal private secretary to the PM and private secretary to Prince William, so I'd seen these interactions up close.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So there's an informal body of experienced people forming a guardianship of the constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I'd say so. But I've come to think it's inadequate. I started out celebrating our unwritten constitution under Lord Hennessy, but I've moved towards wanting a more codified, written constitution. I loathe the 'good chaps' phrase. Historically, those guardians were literally chaps from the same schools and backgrounds. That's not a justifiable way to run a 21st-century G7 economy.

chapters.title: Trust, confidentiality and the golden triangle
chapters.takeaway: The 'golden triangle' of advisers relies on deep trust and confidentiality, which rapid turnover of postholders undermines.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The 'good chaps' phrase hides something important: trust, confidentiality and knowledge. The Cabinet Secretary and the PPSs need private, complex discussions. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Absolutely essential. Just as the PM and sovereign have confidential discussions upstairs, the same must happen downstairs between their advisers. That's why rapid turnover of PPSs and Cabinet Secretaries is a bad idea—it prevents the trusted relationships you need when the constitutional chips are down.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Did you have to educate Prime Ministers on constitutional principles they didn't know?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. Despite their fine educations, some bits were missing.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What are the weaknesses of the Cabinet Secretary as a constitutional guardian? If you couldn't persuade a PM that something was fundamentally wrong, at what point would you resign?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The inherent weakness is that you serve at the PM's pleasure. The PM can ignore your advice and sack you. You could resign in extremis, saying, 'You're not listening on a critical constitutional point.' But in modern politics, a Cabinet Secretary's resignation might not have much impact. We've had so many recently—we come and go like buses. That's another reason I think we need to codify these things rather than rely on a resignation causing a fuss.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Young distinguished between something in a manifesto and something constitutionally offensive. If it's in a manifesto, it's much harder to block.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I agree completely. If an elected PM, backed by Cabinet and Parliament, is carrying out a manifesto commitment, unelected officials pretty much have to get out of the way.

chapters.title: Codifying the constitution: from Cabinet Manual to written constitution
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case wants more codification, including possibly a written constitution, and gives the example of the missing Deputy Prime Minister as a gap.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You've said you want a more codified constitution. Are you thinking of putting conventions into legislation, or a full written constitution? A written constitution would thrust judges into being final arbiters, which concerns me.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I'm at the more radical end—I'd like a written constitution. But I'm pragmatic; it would take a very particular set of circumstances, like a major crisis, to achieve. In the meantime, we could codify more. The Cabinet Manual is woefully out of date. I produced an updated draft three or four Prime Ministers ago, and it's never been published. It has no authority anyway. We could bring parts of it into legislation. For example, we should require a Deputy Prime Minister. After the episode where Boris Johnson might have needed a ventilator, we put arrangements in place to always have a Deputy PM. The Covid inquiry agreed. But the current PM hasn't appointed one. That's a gap—we shouldn't leave the order of precedence to a PM's whim.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What role does the PM's principal private secretary play in constitutional decisions?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The PPS is the most frequent conduit between the Government and the sovereign—the 'no surprises' approach. As PPS, I'd talk to the sovereign's private secretary several times a week about what's going on. The Cabinet Secretary gets involved much less often, usually only when it's a serious constitutional issue. The PPS is critical for the 'no surprises' flow of information.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You mentioned the Deputy PM issue. Historically, the Leader of the House was seen as number two. Now we have a First Secretary of State, Louise Haigh. But it's still in doubt who'd take over if the PM were unavailable. We're making assumptions.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I completely agree. We're a $4 trillion economy, a nuclear power, a P5 nation. We shouldn't be making assumptions about who's in charge if the PM is unavailable. Come on.

chapters.title: Unelected power and the weakness of the monarchy as a safeguard
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case argues that unelected figures, including the monarch, are weak safeguards in extreme circumstances and must ultimately defer to elected government.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: You said unelected people have to get out of the way. What if a government has a narrow majority but a minority of the popular vote? Does that change things?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The principle remains the same. Unelected people—from sovereign to official—have significant power, but they must recognise they're secondary to any elected government. In extreme cases, like exercising prerogative powers, they'd need to be very sure of their ground and take broad advice.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Does that mean the monarchy is a weak constitutional safeguard in extreme circumstances?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In my view, yes.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How should the golden triangle operate if the engine is breaking down?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In 1974 it operated through walks around St James's Park, and those continue. More seriously, when Boris Johnson's team floated calling an election to save him, I was immediately on the phone to other members of the golden triangle, saying we need to step up our DEFCON level. The primary task is exchanging information and triangulating advice so we're all working from the same facts and precedents. But the golden triangle are advisers, not principals. We're support cast to the PM and sovereign.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said the monarch as a safeguard is on the weaker side. Would you strengthen it?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No, I wouldn't strengthen the monarch's role. In a 21st-century democracy, strengthening an unelected Head of State goes against the flow of history. The real backstop should be a written constitution, not Whitehall. I wouldn't put that backstop in the hands of officials.

chapters.title: The journey to a written constitution and its challenges
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case acknowledges the difficulty of achieving a written constitution but believes it's the best long-term safeguard, with some inked lines needed now.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Isn't there a contradiction? You want a written constitution that would define the monarch's role, but you also say the flexibility of the unwritten constitution is its strength.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: This is a classic essay question. I was trained to celebrate the flexibility of our unwritten constitution. But seeing it up close, and considering questions of transparency, who wields power, in whose interests, and how you get rid of them—that's led me to think a written constitution might be the right answer for this country.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Wales operates within a written constitution and it works well. Short of a written constitution, what could strengthen our safeguards?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I'd bring some critical things from the precedent book or Cabinet Manual into legislation. For example, the current change to allow a Roman Catholic or Jewish PM to be involved in appointing Church of England bishops is a significant constitutional move. More seriously, we should clarify the order of precedence—who do you call if X or Y is unavailable? We shouldn't run a country with this level of uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is the constitution overall vulnerable? In what ways?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: We've seen governments ignore precedent and advice drawn from the 'good faith' theory. Things that were pencil lines in our constitution should become inked lines. Leo Amery described the constitution as a living structure, shaped by circumstances. That's a good description. But should we really run a 21st-century G7, P5, nuclear-armed state that way? I'd like a few more inked lines. I'm pragmatic about how to get there—it would take a major crisis to achieve a written constitution, not normal politics. House of Lords reform shows how constitutional tinkering can gum everything up.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Lord Case. We're trying to look ahead 10-15 years at constitutional weaknesses. Anything else you'd like to add?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No. Thank you very much. More power to your elbow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks a lot. I now draw this session to a close.
